page: Vultr vc2-6c-16gb is a Cloud Compute instance featuring 6 shared vCPUs mapped to 3 physical Intel Xeon cores on the x86_64 architecture. The processor operates at a clock speed of 2.0 GHz and includes 16 MB of L3 cache. It is equipped with 16.0 GB of system memory, yielding 2.67 GB per core, and includes 320 GB of local NVMe SSD storage. Network provisioning includes one complimentary public IPv4 address.

Benchmark data indicates a split between single-core and multi-core performance. Single-core stress-ng CPU performance is weak, falling into the bottom 25%, while multi-core performance reaches average levels. Memory read bandwidth is average at 407.68 GB/sec for small cached blocks and 48.31 GB/sec for large uncached blocks, but large block write bandwidth is weak at 18.72 GB/sec. Cryptographic and compression workloads show limitations, with single-threaded gzip and bzip3 decompression scores placing in the bottom 10%.

The shared CPU allocation presents a clear tradeoff, as resource contention can affect sustained single-core execution, as reflected in the low Geekbench single-core score of 796.0. However, the inclusion of 320 GB of local NVMe SSD storage provides a high storage-to-compute ratio for a budget-tier instance. This makes the configuration qualitatively cost-efficient for workloads requiring substantial local storage capacity without demanding continuous, high-performance CPU throughput.

This server configuration is suitable for multi-threaded applications that can tolerate shared CPU scheduling, such as basic web serving, Redis caching (achieving an average of 6.15 million SET operations per second), and light multi-threaded decompression tasks. It is less suited for heavy database operations, software compilation, or large-scale LLM inference, where benchmarks show weak or poor performance.
description: Vultr vc2-6c-16gb is a Cloud Compute instance configured with 6 shared vCPUs on an Intel Xeon x86_64 processor running at 2.0 GHz, paired with 16.0 GB of RAM and 320 GB of local NVMe SSD storage. Its hardware profile delivers a balanced resource density, though the shared CPU allocation introduces performance tradeoffs. Multi-core benchmarks, such as stress-ng and Geekbench ray tracing, achieve average tier results, whereas single-core processing and memory write speeds remain in the lower percentiles. The instance is qualitatively cost-efficient for storage-heavy, non-CPU-intensive workloads. It is best suited for multi-threaded applications, basic web serving, and Redis caching, but is less optimal for intensive database operations or software compilation.
